 Gulf freight rates slump as more ships become available
 By
 Francesca Washtell and John Crowley 
 October 23, 2026 4:00 AM 
 X 
 LinkedIn 
 Facebook 
 Copy link 
 A tanker at the Port of Fujairah. Rates for very large crude carriers have dropped, but are still almost 30 times the daily breakeven level, according to one expert Copyright: Reuters/Amr Alfiky 
 VLCC rates fell 25%
 Additional ships eased pressure
 Hormuz tensions sustain volatility
 Tanker freight rates have fallen by about a quarter from record highs, offering oil buyers a brief respite from soaring shipping costs.
 The Oman-to-China benchmark for very large crude carriers (VLCCs) stood at about $689,000 a day on October 21, down 25 percent from its October 8 peak, shipping news outlet Lloyd’s List reported.
 The market is cooling from an extreme peak , although demand to ship oil remains high. Companies have slowed bookings as more vessels become available, according to Greg Miller, senior reporter at Lloyd’s List .
 “The cure for high prices is high prices,” he told a webinar on Thursday.
 Charterers, the companies that hire ships to transport cargo, have pulled back over the past fortnight, unwilling to keep paying record rates .
 The increase in vessel availability, particularly in the Atlantic, has helped pull prices down, Miller said.
 “The peak rates were just not something that the charterers were willing to keep paying, at least at this stage of the game,” he added.
 Companies with tankers on long-term contracts are also offering them in the spot market, where ships are hired for individual voyages. They believe they can earn more by hiring out the vessels than by using them to move their own oil, Miller said.
 That extra capacity has eased rates. Miller also pointed to a modest dip in ship-to-ship transfers off Oman as Iranian attacks increase .
 Shuttle hustle
 The shuttle system has proved an effective, if expensive, workaround. About 10 million barrels of crude and condensate a day passed through Hormuz in September, mostly on shuttle tankers, according to shipping analytics company Kpler. The estimate excludes Iranian exports.
 Tankers carry crude through the strait, then transfer it to other vessels in the Gulf of Oman for onward delivery.
 The system has helped producers keep oil flowing despite soaring freight rates and insurance costs . But it has tied up ships waiting for ship-to-ship transfers, while irregular arrivals through Hormuz make operations harder to schedule, Miller said.
 High earnings off Oman have also drawn tankers away from the Atlantic, driving up costs there. Some cargos usually carried by the largest vessels have been split among smaller ships, spreading the pressure across the market.
 Strait profits
 Despite the correction, Oman-to-China earnings remain almost 30 times the roughly $25,000 daily breakeven level that Miller cited for VLCCs owned by tanker business Frontline.
 The “super-spike” caused by the sudden surge in Hormuz shuttle flows had been “the icing on the cake” for tanker owners already getting rich, Miller said.
 “The owners still have the cake, and they are still making enormous profits,” he said.
 The security threat remains acute. “This is the highest frequency of attacks against ships in the Strait of Hormuz since the beginning of the conflict,” said Richard Meade, editor-in-chief of Lloyd’s List .
 Miller said rates may have peaked in early October and that “we will never see those numbers again for the rest of our careers”.
 “But not necessarily. No one knows which way rates will go because of geopolitics,” he said.
